text:
👥 Tag 14 | Modul 13: Scaling Workforce Potential Skills I + II
👥 Du kannst KI nicht skalieren, ohne die Menschen zu skalieren, die KI betreiben.

An diesem Tag des CAS AI Scaling an der HWZ Hochschule für Wirtschaft Zürich AG geht es um eine der wichtigsten Fragen der KI Skalierung: Wie bauen Unternehmen die Skills, Rollen und Teams auf, die KI langfristig tragen?

Bisher haben wir Strategie, Value Realization, Architektur, Governance, Security, Agentic Systems, AI Product Management, MLOps, Datenökosystem und Responsible AI betrachtet.

Jetzt geht es um die Menschen dahinter.

Im ersten Teil bauen wir die Lernmaschine der Organisation. Die Kohorte entwirft Lernpfade von AI Literacy bis Advanced Tracks, gestaltet Micro Credentials, Bootcamps und virtuelle Labs und entwickelt Assessment Methoden mit Badge Systemen und Lernfortschritts Dashboards.
Dazu kommen Make or Buy Strategien, Kooperationen mit EdTech und Hochschulpartnern, Employer Branding für AI Rollen und gezielte Recruiting Kampagnen.

Mentoring Netzwerke, Guilds und Communities of Practice sorgen für Wissenstransfer und Bindung. Hackathons und klare Karriereleitern schaffen Motivation und Entwicklung.

Die Schweizer Realität aus 2026: 58 Prozent der Unternehmen nennen Fachkräftemangel als Bremse für KI Innovation, und nur 24 Prozent machen KI Schulungen verpflichtend.

Im zweiten Teil geht es um strategisches Talent Management für AI Rollen.
Denn hinter jeder AI Strategie steckt auch eine Skills und Hiring Strategie.
Die Kohorte führt Skill Gap Analysen durch, leitet künftige Bedarfe ab und definiert Job Blueprints für Rollen wie Prompt Designer, ML Engineer, AI Developer, AI Product Owner, AI Architect und AI Ethics Manager.

Wir analysieren den Arbeitsmarkt für AI Talente, Consulting Rates für externe Spezialist:innen und den Lebenszyklus von Teams nach Tuckman: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing.

Beim Performance Management verbinden wir Vision und OKRs mit individueller Leistung, koppeln diese sauber an AI Model Performance und balancieren Blue Work, also Delivery, und Red Work, also Innovation.
Denn KI Skalierung ist nicht nur eine Technologiefrage. Sie ist eine Workforce Frage.

Dozent:innen für diesen Tag: Mariana Solveig Raschke und Dennis Meier. Sie zeigen euch praxisnah, wie Unternehmen Skills, Rollen, Lernpfade und Talent Management so aufbauen, dass KI nicht an fehlenden Fähigkeiten scheitert.

author: Vikas Kumar
text:
I spent a weekend solving a problem the Karnataka State Police didn't ask me to solve.
KSP Datathon 2026's brief was "conversational AI over the crime database." Everyone builds the same thing: natural language → SQL → results table. I didn't.
Because that assumes the database is clean. It isn't.
Across 1,100+ police stations entering names by hand, one person shows up as Ravi Patil, R. Patil, Patil Ravi, RAVI PATIL, and ರವಿ ಪಾಟೀಲ್ in Kannada. In my dataset, a single repeat offender appears in 21 FIRs under 8 spellings across 17 stations.
Exact-match search finds 2 of them. The other 19 — invisible. No amount of chatbot polish on top recovers a record name-search can't reach. So I attacked the layer underneath: entity resolution.
What I built (solo, zero ML dependencies, deployed on Zoho Catalyst):
→ Syllable-aware Kannada→Latin transliteration
 → A phonetic key tuned for Indian names — not Soundex, which was built for Anglo surnames and fails here
 → IDF-weighted token alignment, so common surnames can't manufacture false links
 → Average-linkage clustering that refuses to chain distinct people through one ambiguous record
Measured against held-out ground truth:
Recall: 99.2% vs 17.9% for exact match — 5.5× more true links recovered
 92.2% fewer comparisons than brute force (blocking → near-linear, scales to state volume)
 15–30ms warm queries
The part I'm proudest of: it refuses when it shouldn't guess. Below its confidence threshold it says "verify manually" instead of fabricating a link. In policing, a false match is wrongful suspicion on a real person — a system that can't say "I don't know" isn't safe to deploy. Every answer ships its reasoning, its provenance, and its limitations.
One honest detail I put in the deck: the residual error is data-limited, not model-limited — some records are genuinely different people with the same name and age, which nothing separates without a corroborating identifier. That's a floor imposed by the data, not the algorithm.
Deterministic AI where mistakes are unacceptable. Generative AI where interaction matters. I think that's the right way to build for a system that has to last a decade.

author: Barry song
text:
The job titles on travel tech careers pages look nothing like they did two years ago.
"Principal Designer, AI Experiences."
"Senior Machine Learning Scientist — GenAI."
"AI Platform Engineer."
"Distinguished Scientist — Agentic AI."
These aren't hypothetical. They're live postings right now — across Booking.com, Skyscanner, Sabre, and Expedia.
Travel companies aren't just adopting AI tools. They're fundamentally rewriting what their engineering teams look like.
The data backs it up. Phocuswright reports 6 in 10 travel companies are now experimenting with or scaling agentic AI. McKinsey found half of organizations using AI expect to hire more data scientists within a year. Travel Tech Talent's 2026 industry analysis shows demand for ML engineers, MLOps specialists, and data platform architects outpacing supply by a widening margin.
Skyscanner reported a 23% productivity boost in engineering teams from generative AI adoption. Flight Centre's chief experience officer said AI competency is now central to how they recruit — not a nice-to-have, a baseline.
What's growing: AI infrastructure, data pipelines, model deployment, automation engineering.
What's quietly shrinking: generalist full-stack roles, UI-focused feature squads, traditional product management.
Here's the part that interests me as someone in recruitment.
The rush to build AI-native teams is real and necessary. But I keep seeing companies treat it as a swap — new AI talent in, domain veterans out — when it should be a merge.
Travel isn't like other tech sectors. The inventory is messy. Supplier relationships are built over years. Distribution networks have layers that no model can infer from a dataset. The people who understand why a rate plan nests inside an ancillary, or why the same hotel appears under three names across two feeds — that knowledge doesn't transfer in an onboarding doc.
The winners in travel tech over the next five years won't be the companies that hire the most AI scientists.
They'll be the ones that figure out how to pair deep industry expertise with AI capability — and keep both in the same room.
Hiring AI talent without retaining domain expertise isn't transformation. It's building a fast engine with no map.
What are you seeing in your industry? Is AI changing your team's composition, or just adding to it?

author: Mohit Rathod, open to work
text:
The distinction between a Data Scientist, an AI Engineer, and an NLP Specialist has widened dramatically. Yet, thousands of aspirants are still applying for all three using the exact same generic resume.  

This is the "Jack of All Trades" trap.  
When you claim to know a little bit of Excel, a bit of PyTorch, some SQL, and Transformer architectures on a single one-page resume, hiring teams don't see a versatile candidate—they see a beginner who hasn't mastered any part of the data lifecycle.  

The modern data ecosystem relies on specialized ownership:  

Infrastructure & Insights (Foundation): Data Engineers build the pipelines to ensure data is clean and reachable, while Data Analysts translate raw numbers into actionable business decisions.  

Predictions & Production (Intelligence): Data Scientists run statistical experiments and predictive modeling, while ML Engineers take those theoretical models and deploy them for millions of users.  

Specialized Frontiers (Perception & Systems): NLP Engineers work directly with Transformers (BERT, GPT), tokenization, and LLMs, while AI Engineers focus on end-to-end system integration and responsible AI practices.  

A generic resume is a rejected resume. Tailoring your projects, portfolio, and tool stack to one specific pillar is the highest-leverage move you can make for your career right now.  

For the hiring managers and senior leads in my network: Have you noticed a shift toward hiring hyper-specialists over generalists in your engineering teams lately, or do you still value broad-spectrum data roles in early-stage setups? Let's discuss in the comments.
